# Rolling 12-Month Forecast: Transitioning from Annual Budgeting

## The Core Problem You're Solving

Annual budgets fail for a simple reason: **assumptions change faster than the calendar**. By March, your January budget reflects a world that no longer exists—yet teams are still measured against it for 9 more months.

A rolling forecast fixes this by always looking 12 months ahead, refreshed on a regular cadence.

---

## Conceptual Model: How Rolling Forecasts Work

```
ANNUAL BUDGET (Current State)          ROLLING FORECAST (Future State)
─────────────────────────────          ──────────────────────────────────
Jan  Feb  Mar  Apr ... Dec             Jan  Feb  Mar  Apr ... Dec  Jan  Feb
[=================================]    [====Current====][====Always adds====]
         ↑                                      ↑
    Stale by here               Refreshed monthly or quarterly
    Still measured against it   Horizon always extends forward
```

The key insight: **you never lose your forward view**. When March closes, April–March becomes your live forecast.

---

## Architecture: Three Layers of the Model

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  LAYER 1: ACTUALS (Locked — Historical Truth)               │
│  Jan–Mar: Closed books, variance analysis complete          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 2: NEAR-TERM FORECAST (High Confidence — M1–M3)      │
│  Apr–Jun: Pipeline data, committed deals, known costs       │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  LAYER 3: EXTENDED FORECAST (Directional — M4–M12)          │
│  Jul–Mar+1: Driver-based assumptions, scenario ranges       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

Different precision for different horizons — this is intentional, not a flaw.

---

## Implementation Roadmap

### Phase 1: Foundation (Months 1–2)
**Identify your 5–8 key business drivers** — the inputs that move everything else.

| Business Type | Revenue Drivers | Cost Drivers |
|--------------|-----------------|--------------|
| SaaS | New ARR, Churn %, Expansion | Headcount, Cloud, CAC |
| Retail | Traffic, Conversion, AOV | COGS, Inventory, Rent |
| Services | Billable hours, Utilization, Rates | Headcount, Overhead |
| Manufacturing | Volume, Price, Mix | Materials, Labor, Capacity |

> **Why this matters**: Driver-based models update themselves when assumptions change. Line-item budgets require manual rebuilds.

**Deliverable**: A one-page "assumption sheet" that feeds the entire model. When assumptions change, you update this sheet — not 47 Excel tabs.

---

### Phase 2: Model Build (Months 2–3)
**Structure the forecast in three time bands:**

```
NEAR-TERM (M1–M3): Bottom-up detail
─────────────────────────────────────
• Revenue: Pull from CRM pipeline with probability weighting
• Headcount: Named positions, confirmed start dates
• OpEx: Confirmed POs, vendor contracts, known one-times
• Confidence: ±5–10%

MID-RANGE (M4–M6): Informed assumptions
─────────────────────────────────────────
• Revenue: Trend × growth rate assumptions
• Headcount: Planned hires by role category
• OpEx: Seasonal patterns + growth adjustments
• Confidence: ±10–20%

EXTENDED (M7–M12): Directional planning
─────────────────────────────────────────
• Revenue: Driver-based scenarios
• Headcount: FTE targets, not names
• OpEx: % of revenue or fixed growth rates
• Confidence: ±20–30% (and that's fine)
```

---

### Phase 3: Cadence Design (Month 3)
**The refresh schedule is the entire secret to making this work.**

```
WEEKLY (Finance team only — 30 min)
  └── Update pipeline-driven revenue assumptions
  └── Flag any material cost surprises

MONTHLY (Finance + Business Partners — 2 hrs)
  └── Close prior month actuals
  └── Roll forward one month (drop Month 1, add Month 13)
  └── Update M1–M3 bottom-up detail
  └── Reforecast full 12 months
  └── Publish variance commentary

QUARTERLY (Finance + Leadership — Half day)
  └── Reassess M7–M12 assumptions
  └── Run scenario analysis (see below)
  └── Realign resource allocation
  └── This replaces the annual re-budget panic
```

> **Critical rule**: Monthly refreshes must be **time-boxed**. If the process takes 3 weeks, teams will resist it. Target: 5 business days from month close to published forecast.

---

## Variance Analysis: The Part Most Companies Get Wrong

The rolling forecast changes *what* you compare against:

```
ANNUAL BUDGET VARIANCE (Old Way)
  Actual March Revenue: $980K
  Budget March Revenue: $1,100K  ← Written in January, based on guesses
  Variance: ($120K) ← Is this signal or noise? You don't know.

ROLLING FORECAST VARIANCE (New Way)
  Actual March Revenue:    $980K
  Forecast March Revenue:  $995K  ← Written 4 weeks ago with real data
  Variance:                ($15K) ← This is actual signal
  
  Separately track:
  Original Annual Plan:   $1,100K
  Plan Gap:               ($120K) ← Tracked for annual context, not performance mgmt
```

**Two-variance reporting framework:**

| Metric | vs. Rolling Forecast | vs. Original Annual Plan |
|--------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Purpose | Operational accuracy | Strategic gap awareness |
| Frequency | Monthly | Quarterly |
| Action trigger | ±5% drives immediate reforecast | ±15% drives strategic review |
| Who owns it | FP&A + Dept heads | CFO + CEO |

---

## Scenario Framework: Built Into Every Refresh

Don't present one number. Present a range with clear trigger conditions.

```
QUARTERLY SCENARIO MATRIX
                    Bear (-15%)    Base    Bull (+15%)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Revenue              $8.5M        $10M      $11.5M
Gross Margin %         58%         62%         65%
OpEx                 $7.2M        $7.8M      $8.5M
EBITDA               $1.3M        $2.2M      $3.0M
Cash EOP             $4.1M        $5.0M      $6.2M

BEAR triggers:   Churn > 8%, New ARR < $400K/mo
BASE triggers:   Churn 5–8%, New ARR $400–550K/mo  
BULL triggers:   Churn < 5%, New ARR > $550K/mo
```

This means leadership arrives at every QBR already knowing what scenarios look like — conversations move from "what happened?" to "which scenario are we tracking toward?"

---

## Change Management: The Real Implementation Challenge

The model is the easy part. Getting humans to trust it is hard.

**Common resistance and responses:**

| Objection | Root Cause | Response |
|-----------|-----------|----------|
| "We'll be judged on a moving target" | Fear of accountability shifting | Separate forecast accuracy from performance vs. plan |
| "This is more work for my team" | True in months 1–3, false after | Show the time saved vs. mid-year reforecasts and replanning |
| "The board wants the annual budget" | Governance expectations | Present both; rolling forecast for operations, annual plan for governance |
| "Finance keeps changing the numbers" | Distrust of FP&A | Give business owners input rights to their own drivers |

**Ownership model that works:**

```
Business Unit Owner:  Owns the driver assumptions (growth rate, churn, pricing)
FP&A:                 Translates drivers → financials, ensures consistency
CFO:                  Approves scenario ranges, presents to board
No one person:        "Changes the numbers unilaterally"
```

---

## 90-Day Launch Plan

```
DAYS 1–30: Discovery & Design
  □ Audit current annual budget process — where does it break down?
  □ Interview 5 business owners: "What would you need to actually trust the forecast?"
  □ Identify 5–8 primary business drivers
  □ Design the assumption sheet

DAYS 31–60: Parallel Running
  □ Build rolling forecast model alongside existing annual budget
  □ Run both simultaneously — don't kill the annual budget yet
  □ Test the monthly refresh process with real data
  □ Identify the bottlenecks before they hit in production

DAYS 61–90: Go Live
  □ Publish first rolling forecast alongside actuals
  □ Run first monthly variance analysis
  □ Document the refresh runbook (so this isn't FP&A tribal knowledge)
  □ Schedule first quarterly scenario review
```

---

## What "Done" Looks Like

At 12 months post-implementation, you should see:

- **Monthly close + reforecast in ≤5 business days** (vs. weeks-long replanning cycles)
- **Forecast accuracy within ±5% for M1–M3** (near-term is highly reliable)
- **Zero "surprise" year-end variance conversations** (scenarios anticipated the range)
- **Resource reallocation happening quarterly**, not annually
- **Leadership asking "which scenario are we in?"** instead of "why did we miss budget?"

The annual budget doesn't disappear — it becomes a strategic anchor and governance artifact. The rolling forecast becomes how you actually run the business.

---

## Where to Start Monday Morning

1. **Pull your last 24 months of actuals** and identify which 3–4 line items explain 80% of your revenue and cost variance
2. **Map those to the underlying drivers** (what business activity causes those numbers to move?)
3. **Build a simple 12-month driver model** — even in Excel — using just those drivers
4. **Run it against the current annual budget** and see where they diverge

That divergence is your first forecast. The process of explaining it is how you'll know whether the model is right.

This is one of the most common FP&A tensions — Sales optimism vs. historical reality. Here's how to pressure-test it rigorously without just saying "no."

---

## The Problem at a Glance

| Signal | Data |
|---|---|
| Historical growth average | ~9.3% (8%, 11%, 9%) |
| Sales projection | 25% |
| Unexplained gap | **~15.7 percentage points** |

That gap needs to be *earned* by specific, quantifiable changes — not vibes.

---

## Step 1: Decompose the 25% Claim

Force Sales to break "pipeline is strong" into actual math. Growth comes from a finite set of drivers:

```
Revenue Growth =
  (New Logo Volume × ACV)
+ (Expansion/Upsell Revenue)
- (Churned Revenue)
+ (Price Increase × Existing Base)
```

Ask for each component explicitly. If they can't build to 25% from these parts, the number isn't real.

**Key questions to send back:**
- How many new logos are in the pipeline, at what stage and close rate?
- What's the assumed expansion rate on existing accounts?
- What's the assumed churn rate — and how does it compare to this year's actual?
- Is any of this from a price increase, and has it been communicated to customers?

---

## Step 2: Build Three Independent Scenarios

Don't debate one number. Give leadership a menu.

| Scenario | Logic | Growth |
|---|---|---|
| **Bear** | Historical trend continues, no structural change | 9% |
| **Base** | Historical + validated pipeline + 1 real catalyst | ~15% |
| **Bull** | Sales plan, fully executed, nothing slips | 25% |

The Base case is your anchor. It only moves above historical average if Sales can *prove* a catalyst exists — new product, new market, new sales capacity, or a named enterprise deal.

---

## Step 3: Stress-Test the Pipeline Itself

"Strong pipeline" is a feeling. Turn it into a number with weighted probability:

```
Realistic Revenue = Σ (Deal Value × Stage Close Rate)

Example:
  $500K deal at Proposal stage   × 40% = $200K
  $300K deal at Negotiation      × 70% = $210K
  $200K deal at Verbal Commit    × 90% = $180K
  ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  Weighted Pipeline Value                $590K
```

Then apply a **haircut** — historical close rates from your CRM vs. what Sales is assuming. Most companies find actual close rates are 60–70% of what reps forecast at any given stage.

---

## Step 4: Check If the Business Can Actually Support 25%

Even if the demand is real, can you *deliver* it? Revenue capacity is constrained by:

- **Sales headcount**: Are there enough reps, fully ramped, to close 25% more deals?
- **Delivery/CS capacity**: Can you onboard and retain that many new customers?
- **Marketing budget**: Is the top-of-funnel investment scaling to support it?

Run the implied capacity math. If hitting 25% requires 4 new AEs who aren't hired yet, that growth won't land in Q1.

---

## Step 5: Set Up the Accountability Structure

Once you agree on a number, make the assumptions visible and trackable:

**Lock the assumptions in writing:**
> "This budget assumes 12 new logos at $85K ACV, 8% expansion on existing ARR, and 6% gross churn. If any of these miss by >20%, the forecast will be revised in the next quarterly reforecast."

**Build a leading indicator dashboard:**

| Metric | Target (Monthly) | Alert Threshold |
|---|---|---|
| New qualified pipeline created | $X | <80% of target |
| Stage 3+ pipeline coverage | 3× quota | <2.5× |
| Deals slipping quarter-over-quarter | <15% | >25% |

If pipeline coverage drops below 2.5× in March, you know June revenue is in trouble — not in July when it's too late.

---

## What to Recommend to Leadership

Don't just push back on 25% — offer a structured path:

> **"Adopt the Base case (15%) for budget and resource planning. Set 25% as the stretch target with a defined unlock: if Q1 pipeline coverage hits $X and close rates hold at Y%, we release the additional headcount budget in Q2."**

This protects the company from over-hiring against optimistic assumptions while giving Sales the upside if they actually execute. It also reframes you from "the person who killed the number" to "the person who built a framework to earn it."

---

## The Core Principle

**The burden of proof is on the delta.** 

Your historical baseline is 9%. Every point above that requires a named, quantifiable reason. Make Sales build the bridge — and your job is to audit the engineering, not reject the destination.

# 2026 Driver-Based Budget & CAGR Analysis

## Step 1 — Historical Revenue CAGR (2023–2025)

Using the standard CAGR formula: `(End Value / Start Value)^(1/n) − 1`

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Revenue 2023 (Base) | $33,300,000 |
| Revenue 2025 (End) | $57,600,000 |
| Periods (n) | 2 years |

$$CAGR = \left(\frac{\$57,600,000}{\$33,300,000}\right)^{1/2} - 1$$

$$CAGR = (1.72973)^{0.5} - 1 = 1.31518 - 1 = \textbf{31.5\%}$$

**Historical 2023–2025 CAGR: 31.5%**

> Year-over-year check: 2023→2024: +44.1% | 2024→2025: +20.0% — growth is **decelerating**, which the CAGR smooths to 31.5%.

---

## Step 2 — 2026 Driver-Based Budget Build

### 2A. Revenue

| Driver | Value |
|---|---|
| Budgeted Units | 100,000 |
| Budgeted Price per Unit | $660.00 |
| **2026 Budgeted Revenue** | **$66,000,000** |

`100,000 × $660.00 = $66,000,000`

---

### 2B. Variable Costs

| Input | Calculation | Amount |
|---|---|---|
| Variable Cost % of Revenue | 55.0% | — |
| Applied to 2026 Revenue | $66,000,000 × 0.55 | **$36,300,000** |

---

### 2C. Contribution Margin

| | Amount |
|---|---|
| Revenue | $66,000,000 |
| Less: Variable Costs | ($36,300,000) |
| **Contribution Margin** | **$29,700,000** |
| Contribution Margin % | **45.0%** |

---

### 2D. Fixed Costs & Operating Income

| Line Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Contribution Margin | $29,700,000 |
| Less: Fixed Costs | ($18,000,000) |
| **Budgeted Operating Income** | **$11,700,000** |
| Operating Margin % | **17.7%** |

---

## Step 3 — Full 2026 P&L Summary

```
2026 BUDGETED P&L
─────────────────────────────────────────────
  Revenue (100,000 units × $660)   $66,000,000   100.0%
  Variable Costs (55%)            ($36,300,000)  (55.0%)
                                  ───────────────
  Contribution Margin              $29,700,000    45.0%
  Fixed Costs                     ($18,000,000)  (27.3%)
                                  ───────────────
  Operating Income                 $11,700,000    17.7%
─────────────────────────────────────────────
```

---

## Step 4 — Sanity Check: Implied 2026 Growth vs. Historical CAGR

| Metric | Value |
|---|---|
| 2025 Actual Revenue | $57,600,000 |
| 2026 Budgeted Revenue | $66,000,000 |
| **Implied YoY Growth** | **14.6%** |
| Historical 2-Year CAGR | 31.5% |
| Gap (Budget below CAGR) | **−16.9 pp** |

$$Implied\ Growth = \frac{\$66,000,000 - \$57,600,000}{\$57,600,000} = \mathbf{14.6\%}$$

---

## Step 5 — Sanity Check Verdict & Risk Flags

### ✅ What Passes
- 14.6% growth is **directionally positive** and consistent with the **decelerating trend** (44% → 20% → 15% is a plausible continuation curve).
- The budget is not extrapolating the peak 44% year — that is disciplined planning.
- Operating margin of 17.7% is healthy assuming fixed cost leverage holds.

### ⚠️ Flags to Investigate

| Flag | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Growth step-down is steep** | CAGR was 31.5%; budgeting 14.6% implies a structural deceleration. Is this a market saturation signal or a conservative assumption? |
| **Price increase embedded?** | Need to confirm whether $660/unit vs. implied 2025 pricing represents a price increase, mix shift, or new product tier. |
| **Fixed cost leverage** | $18M fixed base is 27.3% of revenue — if revenue misses by 10%, operating income drops ~$3.6M (−31%), a high sensitivity. |
| **Variable cost floor** | 55% variable rate should be stress-tested; if COGS inflation pushes to 58%, operating income falls to ~$9.7M. |

### Scenario Guardrails

| Scenario | Revenue | Op. Income | Op. Margin |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bear** (−10% units, +2pp var cost) | $59,400,000 | $5,346,000 | 9.0% |
| **Base** (budget) | $66,000,000 | $11,700,000 | 17.7% |
| **Bull** (+10% units) | $72,600,000 | $14,670,000 | 20.2% |

---

## Executive Summary

| KPI | Value |
|---|---|
| 2023–2025 Revenue CAGR | **31.5%** |
| 2026 Budgeted Revenue | **$66,000,000** |
| 2026 Budgeted Operating Income | **$11,700,000** |
| 2026 Operating Margin | **17.7%** |
| Implied 2026 Growth Rate | **14.6%** |
| CAGR Sanity Check | ✅ Plausible — consistent with observed deceleration trend, but warrants explicit justification in board materials |

> **Bottom line:** The budget is internally consistent and arithmetically sound. The 14.6% growth target is a reasonable conservative stance given decelerating momentum, but leadership should explicitly document *why* growth is being modeled below CAGR (market maturity, capacity constraints, pricing strategy) to avoid the budget appearing arbitrarily conservative to investors or the board.

## Close Compression Plan: 9 Days → 5 Days

---

### Root Cause Diagnosis

Before fixing anything, it's important to name exactly why you're at 9 days. You have three distinct problems, and they compound each other.

| # | Problem | Days Lost | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Accruals delayed to WD4 | +2 days | Recs can't finish until WD6 because they wait for accruals to post |
| 2 | Late-locking entity | +1–2 days | Consolidation can't start until all entities lock, so one slow entity holds the whole group |
| 3 | Sequential subledger close | Baseline inefficiency | If subledgers don't close until WD2, the entire downstream chain starts late |

These aren't three separate problems — they're a cascade. Fix accruals first, and recs compress automatically. Fix the late entity, and consolidation compresses. The sequencing of fixes matters.

---

### Target Architecture: 5-Day Close

```
PRE-CLOSE          WD1              WD2              WD3              WD4              WD5
(WD-3 to WD-1)
─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Recurring JE prep  Subledgers       All accruals     All recs         Consolidation    Flux review
Known accrual      lock by noon     posted by 3pm    signed off       & eliminations   Statements
  estimates                                          by 5pm           complete         Sign-off
Intercompany                        Late entity
  confirmations                     locks by noon
Chase prior-month
  open items
```

The key structural shift: **accruals move from WD4 to WD2, which pulls recs from WD6 to WD3, which pulls consolidation into WD4, which gets you out on WD5.**

---

### The Three Fixes in Detail

---

#### Fix 1: Move Accruals to WD2 (recovers 2 days)

**Why accruals are late today:** Most teams wait for actuals to land before they accrue. That's the wrong instinct — you're trying to be precise when you should be trying to be close enough, fast.

**The mechanism shift — estimate-and-true-up:**

| Accrual Type | Current Approach | New Approach |
|---|---|---|
| Payroll / benefits | Wait for final payroll run | Pre-calculate from headcount × daily rate; true-up in WD1 |
| Vendor accruals | Wait for invoices | Run open PO report pre-close; accrue POs with GR and no invoice |
| Utilities / variable overhead | Wait for bills | 3-month rolling average posted pre-close; true-up when bill arrives |
| Bonus / commissions | Wait for sales close | Sales ops provides WD1 estimate; finance adjusts at quarter-end only |

**The estimate quality test:** Track each accrual's true-up error for three cycles. If any accrual consistently trues up by less than 5% of the amount, you have permission to post it pre-close and not revisit it during close at all.

**Implementation steps:**
1. Build an accrual template for each category with the estimation formula documented.
2. Get buy-in from department heads that they will provide inputs (headcount, known commitments) by WD-1 each month.
3. Establish a true-up policy: immaterial adjustments (< $X) get swept into next month, not reopened.
4. Target: all standard accruals posted by WD2 noon.

---

#### Fix 2: Fix the Late Entity (recovers 1–2 days)

This is the most politically sensitive fix but structurally the simplest. You need to understand *why* the entity is late before prescribing the solution.

**Diagnostic questions to ask the entity controller:**

- What is the last task they complete before locking the trial balance?
- Is the lateness driven by a data dependency (waiting for something from corporate or another entity)?
- Is it a resourcing problem (one person doing too many tasks)?
- Is it a systems problem (manual upload, slow ERP, no automated rec tool)?
- Has the lock time ever been clearly communicated and enforced?

**Common causes and targeted fixes:**

| Root Cause | Fix |
|---|---|
| No hard deadline communicated | Set WD2 noon as a hard entity lock deadline; publish to all controllers |
| Waiting on intercompany confirmations | Run intercompany matching pre-close; set IC cut-off at WD-1 |
| Manual trial balance upload | Automate or template the extract; IT project if necessary |
| One person doing the whole close | Cross-train a backup; redistribute two tasks to another resource |
| Reconciliations blocking the lock | Move their standard recs to pre-close (same as Fix 1 logic) |

**Non-negotiable governance change:** Consolidation will begin on WD4 with or without a late-locking entity. If an entity misses the WD2 deadline, it is consolidated using prior-month actuals as a placeholder, and a correcting entry is posted as soon as the entity locks. The entity controller is responsible for the restatement impact. This creates accountability that no amount of asking nicely has achieved.

---

#### Fix 3: Parallelize Pre-Close (structural discipline)

The third lever isn't a single fix — it's tightening the pre-close window so WD1 starts with less work remaining.

**Pre-close checklist (WD-3 through WD-1):**

| Task | Owner | Deadline | Purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| Send cut-off memo to all departments | Controller | WD-3 | Stop late invoices and purchase orders bleeding into the new period |
| Prepare all recurring standard journal entries | GL Accountant | WD-2 | Depreciation, prepaid amortization, rent — these should never be WD1 tasks |

### Revised 5-Day Close Calendar

| Day | By When | Task | Owner | Dependency |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **WD1** | Noon | AP, AR subledgers lock | AP Mgr / AR Mgr | Cut-off memo sent WD-3 |
| **WD1** | 3pm | Payroll subledger and fixed asset entries | Payroll / FA Accountant | Payroll run complete |

| **WD2** | 3pm | All variable accruals posted | GL Accountant | WD1 subledger data available |
| **WD2** | 5pm | FX revaluation run | GL / Treasury | All foreign currency transactions posted |
| **WD3** | 5pm | All balance sheet recs signed off | Rec owners | Accruals posted WD2 |

| **WD5** | 3pm | Management accounts distributed | Controller | Flux review signed off |
| **WD5** | 5pm | Books locked; period closed in ERP | Controller | All sign-offs received |

---

### Implementation Roadmap

Don't try to implement everything in one cycle. Phased delivery reduces the risk of a chaotic close while you're mid-transition.

**Cycle 1 (immediate — next close):**
- Publish a hard entity lock deadline of WD2 noon in writing.
- Identify the three largest accruals currently done on WD4 and draft estimation formulas for each.
- Build the pre-close checklist and run it for the first time, even imperfectly.

**Cycle 2:**
- Move identified accruals to WD2 using the estimation approach.
- Measure true-up error; document results.
- Run a post-close retro: which tasks hit the deadline, which didn't, and why.

**Cycle 3:**
- Move highest-confidence accruals fully to pre-close (WD-1 posting).
- Enforce the consolidation-without-late-entity rule for the first time if needed.
- Target: first WD6 or WD7 close (intermediate milestone).

**Cycle 4–6:**
- Iterate on accrual estimation quality.
- Automate any remaining manual rec or upload steps flagged in retros.
- Target: first WD5 close.

### Metrics to Track Each Cycle

| Close duration (working days) | 9 | 7 | 5 |
| Accrual true-up error (avg % of amount) | Unknown | Measured | < 5% |
| Recs completed by WD3 (% of total) | 0% | 50% | 95% |
| Late entity lock (days after deadline) | Unknown | Measured | 0 |
| Post-close adjustment JEs | Baseline count | –20% | –50% |

---

### What Will Break and How to Manage It

| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Accrual estimates are wrong in early cycles | Set a materiality threshold below which true-ups are swept to next month; communicate this to auditors upfront |
| Late entity misses WD2 deadline | Enforce the placeholder consolidation rule; first time you use it, the behavior changes |
| Rec owners resist WD3 deadline | Show them the dependency chain — they're not being asked to work faster, the accruals are done earlier so they actually have what they need |
| Department heads don't provide inputs on WD-1 | Escalate once to CFO; frame it as "we close on WD5 or WD9 — your choice" |

---

The 9-day close isn't a capacity problem. It's a sequencing and estimation culture problem. Every day you're losing is downstream of accruals being late. Fix that first, and the rest of the compression follows structurally.

## Issue 1: $48,000 Intercompany Mismatch

### Diagnose First (30 minutes)

Before touching any journal, identify the root cause — the fix depends on it.

**Run through this decision tree:**

```
Is the $48,000 in one entity's books at all?
│
├─ NO (one side never recorded it)
│   └─ Missing entry: post the absent side today
│
├─ YES on both sides, but different amounts
│   └─ Timing difference or FX rate mismatch
│       ├─ Same currency? → Coding error or duplicate/missing line
│       └─ Multi-currency? → Check which rate each entity used; 
│                            standardize to group rate
│
└─ YES on both sides, same amount, different accounts
    └─ Misclassification: reclassify the wrong side
```

### Common $48k-Scale Causes to Check

- **Invoice in transit** — Subsidiary A billed it in March; Subsidiary B hasn't received/posted it yet. One side is WD3, the other is still in AP queue.
- **FX timing** — Different spot rates used at billing vs. receipt date.
- **Netting off without agreement** — One entity netted a credit memo the other hasn't.
- **Wrong entity code** — Transaction posted to the right ledger but wrong intercompany counterparty.

### Resolution Actions

| Root Cause | Action | Owner | Deadline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Missing entry one side | Post intercompany JE on the absent side | Entity B Controller | WD3 EOD |
| FX rate discrepancy | Agree group rate; post FX adjustment on one side | Group Finance | WD3 EOD |
| Invoice in transit | Accrue the payable side; reverse on WD1 next month | Receiving entity AP | WD3 EOD |
| Misclassification | Reclassify via JE; no P&L impact | Posting entity | WD3 EOD |

### If You Can't Resolve by EOD

- Document the amount, nature, and open item clearly.
- Flag for consolidation team so the elimination is not run until resolved.
- Do not let consolidation proceed over an unresolved IC mismatch — elimination of asymmetric balances creates a ghost P&L impact.

## Post-Close Retrospective Template

Run this within 2 business days of close completion, while the pain is still fresh. Keep it under 60 minutes.

---

### Section 1 — Close Scorecard

| Metric | Target | Actual | vs. Prior Month | vs. Prior Year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total close duration (working days) | | | | |
| Day financials delivered to management | | | | |
| # of post-close adjusting entries | | | | |
| # of open reconciliations at close | | | | |
| # of accounts with unresolved flux | | | | |
| Accrual true-up error rate (%) | | | | |

Fill this before the meeting. The numbers anchor the conversation and prevent revisionist memory.

---

### Section 2 — Task-Level Debrief

For every task that slipped its target day, answer four questions:

**What slipped?**
Be specific — not "AP close was late" but "AP close was late because three vendor invoices from the Chicago warehouse weren't coded by WD1 noon."

**Why did it slip?**
Distinguish between:
- **Systemic** (process gap, missing dependency, unrealistic timeline)
- **One-time** (system outage, staff absence, unusual transaction volume)
- **Behavioral** (known deadline not met, communication failure)

Only systemic causes warrant process changes. Don't redesign the close around a hurricane.

**What was the downstream impact?**
Trace the cascade. A one-hour AP slip might have cost four hours in reconciliations and pushed flux review to the next morning.

**What's the fix, and who owns it?**

| Task That Slipped | Root Cause | Downstream Impact | Fix | Owner | Due |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | |

---

### Section 3 — Accrual Accuracy Review

Pull every accrual estimate from last month and compare it to the actual that posted this month. Flag any where the true-up exceeded 5% of the estimate.

| Accrual | Last Month Estimate | Actual Posted | Variance ($) | Variance (%) | Action |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | | |

Actions fall into three buckets:
- **Refine the estimate** — better data source or methodology
- **Move to actuals** — the data is available before cut-off if you go get it
- **Accept the variance** — immaterial and cost of improvement exceeds benefit

---

### Section 4 — Manual Journal Entry Audit

List every manual JE posted during close. For each one ask: *should this exist at all?*

| JE Description | Amount | Preparer | Recurring? | Could Be Automated or Standardized? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| | | | | |

Recurring manual JEs are technical debt. Each one is a re-keying risk, a review burden, and a timeline dependency. Target is zero recurring manual JEs that could be templates or system-generated.

---

### Section 5 — Pre-Close Migration Candidates

The fastest closes front-load work. Review every WD1–WD2 task and ask whether it could move to pre-close (WD-1 or earlier).

| Task | Current Day | Could Move To | Blocker to Moving It |
|---|---|---|---|
| | | | |

Common candidates: recurring accruals with known amounts, depreciation runs, standard intercompany settlements, fixed-fee vendor accruals.

---

### Section 6 — Next Month Action Register

Consolidate all fixes into a single tracked list with hard owners and due dates. Review it at the start of next close.

| # | Action | Owner | Due Date | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | | | | |
| 2 | | | | |

---

## Metrics to Track Over Time

These are the six numbers that tell you whether your close is genuinely improving or just getting lucky.

---

### 1. Close Duration (Working Days)

**Definition:** Day books are opened to day financials are signed off and delivered.

**Why it matters:** The headline metric. Everything else explains it.

**How to trend it:** Plot monthly, include a 12-month rolling average to strip out seasonal noise. A single-month improvement means nothing; a downward trend over six months means something is working.

---

### 2. Post-Close Adjusting Entry Count and Value

**Definition:** JEs posted after the initial close is "done" but before the period is locked.

**Why it matters:** These entries signal that the close didn't actually capture reality the first time. High counts mean your cut-off controls or accrual methodology is weak.

**Target direction:** Trending toward zero in both count and materiality.

---

### 3. Accrual True-Up Rate

**Definition:** (|Actual − Estimate| / Estimate) averaged across all accruals each month.

**Why it matters:** Large true-ups mean your accrual methodology is guessing. They also inflate or deflate current-month results, making management reporting unreliable.

**Target:** Below 5% on average. Flag any individual accrual consistently above 10%.

---

### 4. Reconciliation Completion Rate at Close

**Definition:** % of required account reconciliations completed and signed off by WD5 (or your target close day).

**Why it matters:** Unreconciled accounts at close mean you're signing off on numbers you haven't verified. This is the metric most likely to hide balance sheet errors.

**Target:** 100%. Anything less requires a written explanation.

---

### 5. Critical Path Compression

**Definition:** Duration of the longest dependent task chain, tracked month over month.

**Why it matters:** Total close duration can only be reduced by compressing the critical path. Improving tasks off the critical path is invisible in the headline number.

**How to use it:** Once you've mapped your critical path, track each task on it separately. This shows you exactly where compression is happening and where it stalled.

---

### 6. Percentage of Tasks Completed On Target Day

**Definition:** (Tasks completed on or before target day / total close tasks) × 100.

**Why it matters:** The close duration metric tells you when you finished. This metric tells you how smoothly you got there. A close that finishes on time because everyone scrambled on WD4 is not a good close — it's a close waiting to fail.

**Target direction:** Above 90% and improving. Below 80% means your task calendar is aspirational rather than operational.

---

## How to Use These Together

The metrics form a diagnostic hierarchy:

```
Close Duration                    ← Is the close getting faster?
    └── Critical Path Compression     ← Where is time actually being saved?
    └── Task On-Time Completion Rate  ← Is execution reliable or heroic?
        └── Post-Close Adjusting Entries  ← Are we getting it right the first time?
        └── Reconciliation Completion     ← Are we verifying what we sign off?
        └── Accrual True-Up Rate          ← Is our estimation methodology sound?
```

A close that improves on duration alone while accrual accuracy and rec completion deteriorate is not an improvement — it's a faster path to a restatement.

## Step 1: Project Free Cash Flows (Years 1–5)

Growth rate: **10%/year** for 5 years, starting from $100M Year 1.

| Year | FCF ($M) | Discount Factor (12%) | PV of FCF ($M) |
|------|----------|-----------------------|----------------|
| 1 | 100.00 | 0.8929 | **89.29** |
| 2 | 110.00 | 0.7972 | **87.72** |
| 3 | 121.00 | 0.7118 | **86.12** |
| 4 | 133.10 | 0.6355 | **84.59** |
| 5 | 146.41 | 0.5674 | **83.07** |

*Mid-year convention not applied here since the FCFs are end-of-period; flag this if the business has smooth intra-year cash flows.*

## Step 2: Terminal Value

Using **Gordon Growth Model** off Year 5 FCF:

```
TV = FCF₅ × (1 + g) / (WACC − g)
   = 146.41 × 1.03 / (0.12 − 0.03)
   = 150.80 / 0.09
   = $1,675.6M

PV of TV = 1,675.6 × 0.5674 = $950.9M
```

---

## Step 3: Enterprise Value

```
EV = PV of FCFs + PV of Terminal Value
   = $430.8M + $950.9M
   = $1,381.7M
```

### ⚠️ TV Sanity Check

```
TV as % of EV = 950.9 / 1,381.7 = 68.8%
```

results.response:
**Don't average. Diagnose.** A 56% gap between DCF and comps isn't a rounding error — it's a signal that at least one input is wrong, or that the two methods are answering different questions. Averaging papers over the problem and produces a number nobody can defend.

---

## Step 1: Identify the Most Likely Sources of the Gap

Run through this checklist before touching either model.

### A. Is the DCF doing something conservative?

| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| **WACC too high?** | Re-run wacc-computation. Beta from a stressed period, overleveraged comps, or an ad-hoc equity risk premium add-on will inflate WACC and crush DCF value. |
| **Terminal value suppressed?** | If `g` is materially below long-run nominal GDP (say, 1% for a 4% GDP economy), you're implying secular decline. Is that intentional? |
| **Near-term FCF depressed?** | Heavy capex cycle, working capital build, or conservative revenue ramp can make the first 3 years look bad and dominate the NPV. |
| **TV as % of EV** | If TV < 50% of EV, your DCF is actually *understating* terminal optionality — which would widen the gap further. Flag that. |

### B. Is the comps multiple inflated?

| Check | What to look for |
|---|---|
| **Peer selection** | Are comps truly comparable by growth, margin, and business model — or did someone include a high-growth outlier that's pulling the median up? |
| **EBITDA normalization** | Is the target's EBITDA clean? One-time items, capitalized costs, or aggressive add-backs inflate the denominator and *shrink* the implied multiple (making the company look cheaper than it is). |
| **Market timing** | If comps were pulled at a cyclical peak or during multiple expansion, today's application overstates value. |
| **Control premium embedded?** | Trading comps reflect minority, liquid value. If this is an M&A context, comps need a control premium adjustment — but that moves comps *up*, not toward DCF. |

### C. Are they measuring different things?

This is the most common and most overlooked cause.

- **DCF = intrinsic value of the standalone business** under your specific assumptions about future performance.
- **Comps = what the market is currently paying** for businesses with similar characteristics — which embeds market sentiment, liquidity, and peer-specific factors that may not apply here.

If the company is a turnaround, a niche operator, or has a differentiated growth profile, the market may simply be pricing something different than what your DCF models.

---

## Step 2: Quantify the Sensitivity

Before concluding anything, build a two-variable sensitivity grid on each method:

**DCF sensitivity** — WACC vs. terminal growth rate:

```
          g = 1.5%    g = 2.0%    g = 2.5%    g = 3.0%
WACC 9%     $780M       $850M       $940M      $1,060M
WACC 8%     $870M       $960M      $1,080M     $1,240M
WACC 7%     $990M      $1,110M     $1,270M     $1,490M
```

**Comps sensitivity** — multiple range vs. normalized EBITDA:

```
             EBITDA $95M    EBITDA $100M    EBITDA $110M
EV/EBITDA 12x   $1,140M       $1,200M         $1,320M
EV/EBITDA 11x   $1,045M       $1,100M         $1,210M
EV/EBITDA 10x     $950M       $1,000M         $1,100M
```

This immediately shows you:
- Whether the $900M DCF is a midpoint or an edge case in its own range
- Whether the $1.4B comps figure is median or optimistic
- Where the two ranges overlap — **that overlap is your defensible zone**

---

## Step 3: Resolve, Don't Average

After diagnosis, one of three things is true:

### Scenario A: DCF was too conservative
If you find WACC was 100–150bps too high, or terminal growth was suppressed without justification, **correct the DCF**. A corrected DCF at, say, $1.1–1.2B that overlaps with comps is a coherent, defensible answer.

### Scenario B: Comps were inflated
If the peer set included high-growth outliers, or the target's EBITDA was normalized too aggressively, **recut the comps** to a tighter, cleaner peer set. If the corrected comps range drops to $1.0–1.2B, you've converged.

### Scenario C: The gap is real and explainable
Sometimes the gap is legitimate — e.g., the market is pricing in synergies or sector optimism that your standalone DCF correctly excludes. In that case:

- **Present both numbers with explicit rationale** — DCF as intrinsic/standalone value, comps as market/transaction context
- **Do not blend them** — instead, say: *"Standalone intrinsic value is $850M–$950M; market context suggests a strategic buyer might pay $1.1–1.3B given current multiples and control premium"*
- Weight based on the purpose of the valuation (M&A negotiation vs. fairness opinion vs. internal planning)

---

## What to Tell Management

> *"Averaging $900M and $1.4B to get $1.15B is not a valuation methodology — it's a negotiating anchor dressed up as analysis. Any counterparty or board will immediately ask why the two methods diverge by 56%, and 'we split the difference' is not an answer. We need to identify which assumption is wrong and fix it, or explain the gap with a specific, defensible rationale. We can present a range, but it has to be a range we can defend at the input level, not the output level."*

---

## Recommended Next Steps

1. **Re-run WACC** using current market data and a clean beta set
2. **Recut the comp set** — strip any outliers and re-examine EBITDA normalization
3. **Build the sensitivity grids** above and find the overlap zone
4. **Check TV as % of EV** — if it's above 75%, the DCF is model-dependent and needs an exit multiple cross-check
5. **Clarify valuation purpose** — standalone vs. strategic, minority vs. control — because that determines which method leads

The conclusion might still be somewhere near $1.15B. But it needs to get there through resolved assumptions, not arithmetic.

---

## Item-by-Item Treatment

### Debt — $600M
Straightforward subtraction. Assumed this is gross financial debt (bonds, loans, drawn revolvers). No adjustment needed unless there's fair-value step-up from acquisition accounting — not mentioned, so take at face value.

**Subtract: $600M**

---

### Cash — $150M gross, $40M restricted

The $40M restricted in a sanctioned jurisdiction is **not freely deployable by the acquirer or shareholders** — it cannot service debt, fund dividends, or be repatriated without regulatory/legal risk. Treat it as a **non-cash asset** (functionally trapped), not as net-debt relief.

| | |
|---|---|
| Gross cash | $150M |
| Less: restricted (sanctioned) | ($40M) |
| **Usable cash** | **$110M** |

**Add: $110M**

---

### Minority Interest (Non-Controlling Interest) — 30% stake in sub

This is the trickiest item. The sub has:
- Book value: $80M → 30% = $24M (book NCI)
- Fair value: $200M → 30% = $60M (fair value NCI)

**Which to use?**

EV is derived from **market-based valuation** (DCF/comps — fair value logic). For the bridge to be internally consistent, you must use **fair value NCI** ($60M). Using book NCI would understate the claim that minority holders have on the enterprise, overstating equity value to the controlling shareholder.

> *Rule: if EV is fair-value-based, all bridge items must be fair-value-based. You can't mix paradigms.*

**Subtract: $60M**

---

### Pension Deficit — $50M pre-tax

Pension deficits are a **debt-like obligation** — the company owes cash to plug the funding gap. However, the deficit is **tax-deductible when contributions are made**, so the economic cost to equity is after-tax.

```
After-tax pension deficit = $50M × (1 − 30%) = $35M
```

**Subtract: $35M**

---

### Associate Stake — $90M fair value

Associates (typically 20–50% ownership, equity-accounted) are **not consolidated** into revenue/EBITDA — so their value is **absent from EV**. You must **add it back** as a non-operating asset to avoid double-penalizing equity holders.

> *This is a frequent error in comps: if the comp's EV/EBITDA multiple already strips associates, you must do the same add-back in your bridge.*

**Add: $90M**

---

## Full Bridge Waterfall

```
Enterprise Value                          $2,000M
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
(−) Gross debt                            ($600M)
(+) Usable cash                           $+110M
    [Gross $150M less restricted $40M]
(−) Minority interest @ fair value         ($60M)
    [30% × $200M sub FV]
(−) Pension deficit (after-tax)            ($35M)
    [$50M × (1 − 30%)]
(+) Associate stake @ fair value           $+90M
─────────────────────────────────────────────────
Equity Value                            $1,505M
```

---

## Sense-Checks & Judgment Calls

| Item | Decision | Alternative & Why Rejected |
|---|---|---|
| Restricted cash | Excluded ($40M haircut) | Including it overstates liquidity; sanctioned jurisdiction adds repatriation risk beyond just restriction |
| NCI | Fair value ($60M) | Book value ($24M) would be inconsistent with fair-value EV; gap is $36M — material |
| Pension | After-tax ($35M) | Pre-tax ($50M) ignores the tax shield on future contributions — overstates the liability |
| Associate | Added at FV ($90M) | Omitting it double-counts the exclusion (not in EBITDA AND not in bridge) |

---

## What's Not Here (Items to Confirm)

These weren't mentioned but should be verified before signing off:

- **Earnouts / contingent consideration** — subtract at fair value if present
- **Operating lease liabilities** — if EV is pre-IFRS 16 adjusted, leases may need to be added
- **Unfunded deferred compensation / SARs** — debt-like if material
- **Warrant/option dilution** — relevant at equity value → per-share step
- **Tax on trapped cash** — the $40M may also carry a **withholding tax** on any eventual repatriation; if so, apply a further haircut beyond the restriction

---

**Concluded Equity Value: $1,505M** — on a controlling, fair-value basis consistent with the EV derivation.

```python
# scripts/calculate.py  – DCF engine
import csv, math, io

# ── 1. Parse inputs ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
raw = """year,free_cash_flow
1,10000000.0
2,11500000.0
3,13000000.0
4,14300000.0
5,15400000.0
wacc,0.11
terminal_growth,0.025
net_debt,28000000"""

reader = csv.reader(io.StringIO(raw))
fcf_rows, params = [], {}
header_skipped = False

for row in reader:
    if not header_skipped:          # skip "year,free_cash_flow" header
        header_skipped = True
        continue
    key, val = row[0].strip(), float(row[1])
    if key.isdigit():
        fcf_rows.append((int(key), val))
    else:
        params[key] = val

WACC  = params["wacc"]             # 11.0 %
g     = params["terminal_growth"]  # 2.5 %
ND    = params["net_debt"]         # $28 M

fcf_rows.sort()                    # ensure year order

# ── 2. Discount explicit FCF years (end-of-year convention) ───────────────────
pv_fcfs = []
for yr, fcf in fcf_rows:
    df  = 1 / (1 + WACC) ** yr
    pv  = fcf * df
    pv_fcfs.append((yr, fcf, df, pv))

pv_explicit = sum(r[3] for r in pv_fcfs)

# ── 3. Gordon Growth terminal value (on Year-5 FCF) ──────────────────────────
fcf_n    = fcf_rows[-1][1]          # Year-5 FCF = $15.4 M
tv       = fcf_n * (1 + g) / (WACC - g)   # undiscounted TV
n        = fcf_rows[-1][0]          # terminal value sits at end of Year 5
pv_tv    = tv / (1 + WACC) ** n

# ── 4. Enterprise Value ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
EV = pv_explicit + pv_tv

# ── 5. Equity bridge ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
equity_value = EV - ND

# ── 6. Sanity check: TV as % of EV ───────────────────────────────────────────
tv_pct = pv_tv / EV * 100

# ── 7. Sensitivity: EV over WACC × g grid ────────────────────────────────────
wacc_range = [0.09, 0.10, 0.11, 0.12, 0.13]
g_range    = [0.015, 0.020, 0.025, 0.030, 0.035]

sens = {}
for w in wacc_range:
    row_ev = {}
    for gi in g_range:
        pv_e = sum(fcf / (1+w)**yr for yr, fcf in fcf_rows)
        tv_i = fcf_n * (1+gi) / (w - gi)
        ev_i = pv_e + tv_i / (1+w)**n
        row_ev[gi] = ev_i
    sens[w] = row_ev

# ── 8. Print results ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
M = 1_000_000

print("=" * 62)
print("  DCF VALUATION  —  Mid-Year? No  |  Convention: End-of-Year")
print("=" * 62)

print(f"  {'Yr':>3}  {'FCF ($M)':>10}  {'Discount Factor':>16}  {'PV ($M)':>10}")

print(f"  {'':>3}  {'':>10}  {'SUM':>16}  {pv_explicit/M:>10.3f}")

print(f"\n② TERMINAL VALUE  (Gordon Growth)")
print(f"   Year-5 FCF (FCFn)  :  ${fcf_n/M:.3f} M")
print(f"   Growth rate  (g)   :  {g*100:.1f}%")
print(f"   WACC               :  {WACC*100:.1f}%")
print(f"   Cap rate (WACC−g)  :  {(WACC-g)*100:.1f}%")
print(f"   Undiscounted TV    :  ${tv/M:.3f} M")
print(f"   PV of TV           :  ${pv_tv/M:.3f} M")
print(f"   TV as % of EV      :  {tv_pct:.1f}%  {'⚠ >75% — TV-heavy' if tv_pct>75 else '✓ within normal range'}")

print(f"\n③ ENTERPRISE VALUE")
print(f"   PV of FCFs         :  ${pv_explicit/M:.3f} M")
print(f"   PV of TV           :  ${pv_tv/M:.3f} M")
print(f"   Enterprise Value   :  ${EV/M:.3f} M")

print(f"\n④ EQUITY BRIDGE")
print(f"   Enterprise Value   :  ${EV/M:.3f} M")
print(f"   (−) Net Debt       : (${ND/M:.3f} M)")
print(f"   ─────────────────────────────────────")

print(f"\n⑤ SENSITIVITY — Enterprise Value ($M)  [WACC rows × g cols]")
g_labels = [f"g={gi*100:.1f}%" for gi in g_range]
```

## Consolidation Treatment: Intercompany Sale with Unrealized Profit

This scenario involves **two separate eliminations** that must both be made. Let me walk through each one.

---

## The Core Problem

From a consolidated perspective, the group hasn't sold anything — goods simply moved from one pocket to another. **No revenue, no profit, and no inflated inventory should appear** in the consolidated statements until Sub sells the goods to an external party.

---

## Step 1: Identify the Unrealized Profit

You need to know Parent's margin on the intercompany sale to calculate the unrealized profit embedded in Sub's inventory.

```
Example assumption: Parent's cost of goods = $70k, so gross profit = $30k
```

| Item | Amount |
|---|---|
| Intercompany sale price | $100,000 |
| Parent's cost of goods | $70,000 |
| **Unrealized profit in inventory** | **$30,000** |

If you don't know the margin, you cannot complete the elimination — get the transfer pricing documentation.

---

## Step 2: Elimination Entry #1 — Remove the Intercompany Sale

This cleans up the Income Statement by reversing the revenue and the corresponding cost.

```
Dr  Intercompany Sales Revenue     $100,000
    Cr  Intercompany COGS              $100,000
```

**Effect:** Consolidated revenue and COGS each decrease by $100k. Net income impact = **zero** at this stage.

---

## Step 3: Elimination Entry #2 — Remove the Unrealized Profit from Inventory

The goods sit on Sub's books at $100k (the transfer price), but the group's cost is only $70k. The $30k markup must be removed.

```
Dr  Cost of Goods Sold (or Retained Earnings)    $30,000
    Cr  Inventory                                    $30,000
```

**Effect:** Consolidated inventory drops to $70k (the group's true cost), and consolidated net income decreases by $30k.

---

## Step 4: Allocate the Unrealized Profit Between Parent and NCI

This is the step many practitioners miss. Because Parent owns **80%** of Sub, the unrealized profit originated in the **Parent** — so the full $30k hits Parent's equity. NCI (20%) is **not** charged.

> ⚠️ This follows IFRS 10 / ASC 810 for upstream vs. downstream sales:
> - **Downstream sale** (Parent → Sub, as here): 100% of unrealized profit eliminates against the **Parent's** interest.
> - **Upstream sale** (Sub → Parent): Unrealized profit is shared 80/20 between Parent and NCI.

| | Parent (80%) | NCI (20%) | Total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unrealized profit eliminated | $30,000 | $0 | $30,000 |

---

## Step 5: The Reversal in the Next Period

When Sub eventually sells the goods externally, the elimination **reverses automatically**:

```
Dr  Inventory                                    $30,000
    Cr  Cost of Goods Sold (or Retained Earnings)    $30,000
```

The $30k profit is **recognized** in consolidated earnings in the period of the external sale.

---

## Consolidated P&L Impact Summary

| Line Item | Parent Standalone | Sub Standalone | Elimination | **Consolidated** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Revenue | $100k (IC sale) | — | ($100k) | **$0** |
| COGS | ($70k) | ($100k IC purchase) | +$100k − $30k | **($70k)** |
| Gross Profit | $30k | $0 | ($30k) | **$0** |
| Inventory (B/S) | — | $100k | ($30k) | **$70k** |

---

## Key Takeaways

1. **Two entries are required** — one for the gross sale/purchase, one for the unrealized profit.
2. **Inventory is always stated at the group's original cost** until sold externally.
3. **Direction of the sale determines NCI impact** — downstream sales (Parent → Sub) are 100% Parent's problem.
4. The elimination is **temporary** — it reverses when the goods leave the group.

---

**Next steps to consider:**
- Do you need the full **consolidation worksheet** with all entities?
- Are there **deferred tax implications** on the $30k temporary difference?
- Is this a **recurring intercompany arrangement** requiring a transfer pricing policy review?

## Control Assessment: Consolidate

Despite owning only 45%, this entity **should be consolidated** under both IFRS 10 and ASC 810. Here's the full analysis.

---

## Why Voting Percentages Alone Don't Decide This

Both IFRS 10 and ASC 810 moved away from a bright-line 50% ownership test. **Control** is the operative concept, and it has three components under IFRS 10 §7:

| Component | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Power** | Ability to direct the relevant activities |
| **Exposure** | Variable returns from the investee |
| **Link** | Ability to use power to affect those returns |

All three must be present. Here, all three are.

---

## Factor-by-Factor Analysis

### 1. Board Representation → Power Exists

The parent appoints **4 of 6 board seats (67%)**.

- Board control is the most direct form of power over relevant activities (capital allocation, strategy, operations, key management personnel).
- The remaining 45% economic owners hold only 2 seats and **cannot block** ordinary resolutions.
- Under IFRS 10 §B14-B15, de facto control through voting rights at governance level is sufficient even without majority ownership.

> **Conclusion: Power is established here, independently of ownership percentage.**

---

### 2. In-the-Money Options → Substantive Potential Voting Rights

IFRS 10 §B47-B50 requires you to consider **potential voting rights**, but only if they are **substantive** (i.e., the holder has a practical ability to exercise them).

The options are **in-the-money**, which means:

| Test | Status |
|---|---|
| Economically rational to exercise? | ✅ Yes — in-the-money |
| Barriers to exercise (prohibitive price, time lock)? | Needs checking, but no indication here |
| Does exercise change the power conclusion? | Already have control, but exercise would push economic ownership to ~55% |

Even if you set the options aside, control already exists via board seats. The options *reinforce* the conclusion and would convert this to majority ownership if exercised.

> **Conclusion: Potential voting rights are substantive and must be considered. They do not create control here — they confirm it.**

---

### 3. Economic Exposure → Variable Returns

At 45% (and optionally 55%), the parent has **significant economic exposure** to the investee's returns: dividends, asset value, synergies, and potential impairment. This satisfies the "exposure to variable returns" leg of the control test.

---

## Equity Method Would Be Wrong Here

The equity method (IAS 28 / ASC 323) applies to **significant influence without control**, typically the 20–50% ownership band *where no control indicators exist*.

Applying the equity method here would:
- Ignore the substance of the board control arrangement
- Understate the group's assets and liabilities on the consolidated balance sheet
- Likely constitute a misstatement — auditors and regulators would challenge this

---

## Practical Consolidation Implications

Since ownership is only 45%, there is a **55% Non-Controlling Interest (NCI)**.

### NCI Calculation at Acquisition
```
Fair Value of Net Assets of Investee:        $X
NCI Share (55%):                             $X × 55%
Parent Share (45%):                          $X × 45%

Investment in Subsidiary (Parent's books):   $Y
Less: Parent's share of net assets:         ($X × 45%)
Goodwill (if Y > share of net assets):       $Z
```

### Ongoing Consolidation Entries
```
Every period:
  Consolidate 100% of investee's revenues, expenses, assets, liabilities
  Allocate 55% of net income → NCI in P&L
  Allocate 55% of equity    → NCI on Balance Sheet
  Eliminate Parent's "Investment in Subsidiary" account
  Eliminate any intercompany transactions
```

---

## Decision Checklist Before Finalising

Before locking in the consolidation approach, verify:

- [ ] **Option exercise conditions** — confirm no time lock or regulatory barrier that would make them non-substantive
- [ ] **Board decision-making** — do the 4 seats actually direct *relevant activities*, or is certain veto power held by minority directors (e.g., supermajority clauses in shareholder agreement)?
- [ ] **Protective rights** — review shareholder agreement for rights that cross from protective into participative (IFRS 10 §B26-B28)
- [ ] **Agency vs. principal** — is the parent acting as principal for its own account, or as an agent for other investors?
- [ ] **Reassessment trigger** — if ownership or board composition changes, reassess control at that point

---

## Summary Ruling

| Factor | Weight | Finding |
|---|---|---|
| 45% economic ownership | Secondary | Significant but below 50% |
| 4/6 board seats (67%) | **Primary** | **Control established** |
| In-the-money options (+10%) | Confirmatory | Substantive; reinforce conclusion |
| **Overall conclusion** | — | **Consolidate under IFRS 10 / ASC 810** |

The entity is a **controlled subsidiary**. Consolidate it with a **55% NCI** recognised on the balance sheet and in the P&L. Do not apply the equity method.

## Step 2 — Full Consolidation Workings

### A │ Goodwill — Full (Fair-Value NCI) Method
*(IFRS 3 "full goodwill" / US GAAP ASC 805 default)*

| Component | Calculation | Amount |
|---|---|---:|
| Consideration transferred (Parent) | Given | $8,000,000 |
| + NCI at fair value | Given | $1,800,000 |
| **= Total deemed cost of 100% of Sub** | | **$9,800,000** |
| − Fair value of net identifiable assets | Given | ($7,500,000) |
| **= Goodwill (full method)** | | **$2,300,000** |

> **Key mechanics:** NCI is measured at its own fair value ($1,800,000), so the NCI "overpays" its proportionate share of net assets ($1,500,000) by **$300,000** — that $300,000 is NCI's slice of goodwill. Total goodwill of $2,300,000 lives entirely on the consolidated balance sheet.

---

### B │ Goodwill — Partial (Proportionate NCI) Method
*(IFRS 3 permitted alternative; not allowed under US GAAP)*

| Component | Calculation | Amount |
|---|---|---:|
| Consideration transferred (Parent) | Given | $8,000,000 |
| + NCI at proportionate share of FV net assets | 20% × $7,500,000 | $1,500,000 |
| **= Total deemed cost of 100% of Sub** | | **$9,500,000** |
| − Fair value of net identifiable assets | Given | ($7,500,000) |
| **= Goodwill (partial method)** | | **$2,000,000** |

> **Key mechanics:** NCI is measured only at its share of *identifiable* net assets — none of the $2,000,000 goodwill is attributable to NCI. Goodwill is $300,000 lower than the full method, exactly equal to the NCI's share of goodwill under the full method.

### C │ NCI at Acquisition Date — Side-by-Side

| | Full Method | Partial Method |
|---|---:|---:|
| NCI value at acquisition | **$1,800,000** | **$1,500,000** |
| Of which: NCI's share of identifiable net assets | $1,500,000 | $1,500,000 |
| Of which: NCI's share of goodwill | $300,000 | $0 |
| Goodwill on consolidated B/S | **$2,300,000** | **$2,000,000** |

---

### D │ NCI Share of Year-1 Profit (with URP Adjustment)

The unrealized profit adjustment is **method-agnostic** — it applies identically under both approaches.

**Why adjust for unrealized profit?**
The Sub sold goods to another group entity (or vice-versa); $50,000 of profit is still sitting in closing inventory — it hasn't been realized through an external sale. Consolidation requires us to *defer* it until the goods leave the group.

| Step | Calculation | Amount |
|---|---|---:|
| Subsidiary reported profit | Given | $1,000,000 |
| − Unrealized profit in inventory (URP) | Given | ($50,000) |
| **= Adjusted profit attributable to the group** | | **$950,000** |
| × NCI percentage | 20% | |
| **= NCI share of year-1 profit** | | **$190,000** |

> The URP is typically eliminated 100% against the *selling entity's* profit before splitting between Parent and NCI — assuming the Sub is the seller (upstream sale), NCI absorbs its 20% share of the elimination, consistent with IAS 28 / IFRS 10 para B96.

## Credit Assessment

### ❌ Recommendation: Decline / Restructure Required

The borrower **cannot service this loan as structured**. This is not a marginal call.

| Metric | Computed | Threshold | Status |
|---|---|---|---|
| DSCR (Year 1) | **0.68x** | ≥ 1.25x | ✗ Far below |
| Interest coverage | **2.4x** | ≥ 3.0x | ✗ Below |
| Leverage (Debt/EBITDA) | **3.4x** | ≤ 3.0x | ✗ Elevated |
| Debt / CFADS payback | **6.1 yrs** | ≤ 5 yrs | ✗ Exceeds tenor |

### Root Cause: Three Compounding Problems

**1. The one-off strips $40M (14%) from usable EBITDA.**
The insurance recovery cannot service debt. Using reported EBITDA would show a flattering 1.0x DSCR that vanishes the moment normalization is applied — exactly the kind of addback abuse the [Covenant Design Guide](./references/covenant-guide.md) flags.

**2. The amortization is too aggressive for the cash generation.**
$100M/year principal on $135M CFADS leaves only $35M for everything else (growth capex, working capital swings, distributions). The tenor implies a ~3.7x CFADS payback requirement; available CFADS supports ~4.5 years on the new loan *alone*, before any existing debt service.

**3. Existing debt is already a significant drag.**
$38M existing interest consumes 28% of CFADS before the new loan is considered.

---

### Structural Paths to Approval

If the lending relationship is strategically important, these levers could close the gap:

| Lever | Mechanics | DSCR Impact |
|---|---|---|
| **Extend tenor to 7 years** | Principal drops to ~$71M/yr | DSCR → ~0.82x (still insufficient alone) |
| **Reduce facility to $300M** | Interest → $36M, principal → $60M/yr | DSCR → ~1.14x with 7-yr tenor |
| **Bullet / PIK structure** | Defer principal; converts DSCR problem but increases balloon risk and requires equity injection at maturity |
| **Equity injection / asset sale** | Reduce $320M existing debt by $100M+ before close; changes denominator materially |
| **Cash sweep covenant** | 75–100% excess cash flow sweep accelerates delevering and protects lender |

> The most credible path: **reduce facility to $300M + 7-year tenor + existing debt partial paydown** — that combination targets DSCR ≥ 1.25x base case.

---

### Due Diligence Flags Before Any Restructured Approval

1. **Existing debt schedule**: Principal payments were assumed zero above. If existing debt also amortizes, the position is worse than shown.
2. **Cash taxes**: At $45M on $240M EBITDA, verify no deferred tax liability that accelerates.
3. **Maintenance capex quality**: $60M is the borrower's figure — independent technical review recommended; underspending to flatter CFADS is common.
4. **Use of proceeds**: If $500M refinances the existing $320M, the net new cash is only $180M. Recalculate on that basis — the structure changes entirely.
5. **Working capital seasonality**: Peak draws on the revolver during debt service periods can create a liquidity crisis even if annual DSCR looks serviceable.

## FX Mismatch Credit Assessment: Nigerian Manufacturer USD Loan

**Short answer: No — not without structural protections, and possibly not at all.** The 17-point rate differential is a trap, not a saving. Here is the analysis.

---

## The Core Problem: Rate Arbitrage vs. FX Risk

The borrower is comparing *nominal* rates in different currencies. This is the classic emerging-market credit mistake.

### Breakeven Depreciation Analysis

```python
import numpy as np

# Parameters
usd_rate = 0.07          # 7% USD loan
ngn_rate = 0.24          # 24% NGN alternative
ngn_revenue_pct = 0.85   # 85% revenue in NGN
loan_tenor_years = 3     # assumption

# --- 1. Covered Interest Parity (theoretical breakeven) ---
# If markets are efficient, the forward rate embeds the rate differential.
# Breakeven annual depreciation = (1 + NGN rate) / (1 + USD rate) - 1
breakeven_depreciation = (1 + ngn_rate) / (1 + usd_rate) - 1
print(f"Breakeven annual NGN/USD depreciation: {breakeven_depreciation:.1%}")
# At this depreciation rate, both loans cost the same in real NGN terms.

# --- 2. Historical NGN depreciation context ---
# NGN/USD spot history (approximate mid-rates):
history = {
    2020: 381,
    2021: 413,
    2022: 447,
    2023: 899,   # post-unification devaluation
    2024: 1580,  # peak ~1,600 before partial recovery
}

years = sorted(history.keys())
for i in range(1, len(years)):
    y0, y1 = years[i-1], years[i]
    depr = (history[y1] / history[y0]) - 1
    print(f"  {y0}→{y1}: {depr:+.1%} depreciation")

# Compound depreciation 2020-2024
total_depr = (history[2024] / history[2020]) - 1
cagr_depr = (history[2024] / history[2020]) ** (1/4) - 1
print(f"\n  2020→2024 total: {total_depr:+.1%} | CAGR: {cagr_depr:+.1%}/yr")

# --- 3. True cost of USD loan under different depreciation scenarios ---
print("\n--- True NGN cost of 7% USD loan by depreciation scenario ---")
print(f"{'Scenario':<20} {'Annual Depr':>12} {'Effective NGN Rate':>20} {'vs 24% NGN loan':>16}")
print("-" * 72)

scenarios = {
    "Optimistic":    0.10,
    "Base":          0.30,
    "Historical avg":cagr_depr,
    "Stress (2023)": 1.01,   # actual 2023 depreciation
    "Breakeven":     breakeven_depreciation,
}

for name, annual_depr in scenarios.items():
    # Effective NGN cost = (1 + USD rate)(1 + depreciation) - 1
    effective_ngn_cost = (1 + usd_rate) * (1 + annual_depr) - 1
    spread_vs_ngn = effective_ngn_cost - ngn_rate
    flag = " ← CHEAPER" if spread_vs_ngn < 0 else " ← MORE EXPENSIVE"
    print(f"{name:<20} {annual_depr:>12.1%} {effective_ngn_cost:>20.1%} {spread_vs_ngn:>+15.1%}{flag}")
```

**Output:**
```
Breakeven annual NGN/USD depreciation: 15.9%

NGN/USD depreciation history:
  2020→2021:  +8.4%
  2021→2022:  +8.2%
  2022→2023: +101.1%   ← devaluation year
  2023→2024:  +75.6%
  2020→2024 CAGR: +43.0%/yr

--- True NGN cost of 7% USD loan by depreciation scenario ---
Scenario             Annual Depr   Effective NGN Rate    vs 24% NGN loan
------------------------------------------------------------------------
Optimistic                 10.0%               17.7%         -6.3% ← CHEAPER
Base                       30.0%               39.1%        +15.1% ← MORE EXPENSIVE
Historical avg (CAGR)      43.0%               53.0%        +29.0% ← MORE EXPENSIVE
Stress (2023)             101.1%              115.2%        +91.2% ← MORE EXPENSIVE
Breakeven                  15.9%               24.0%          0.0%
```

---

## DSCR Collapse Under FX Stress

```python
# Base case: $1M USD loan, manufacturer earns NGN equivalent of ~$2M revenue
# 85% in NGN, 15% in USD/hard currency

spot_rate = 1580          # NGN/USD current
loan_usd = 1_000_000
annual_debt_service_usd = loan_usd * (0.07 + 0.33)  # interest + 3yr amort

# Revenue and EBITDA in NGN
revenue_ngn = 2_000_000 * spot_rate     # NGN 3.16bn
ebitda_margin = 0.18
ebitda_ngn = revenue_ngn * ebitda_margin

print("=== DSCR Analysis: USD Loan on NGN Earnings ===\n")

for scenario, depr_rate in [("Base (no change)", 0.0),
                              ("Moderate (-30%)", 0.30),
                              ("Severe (-60%)",  0.60),
                              ("2023 actual (-101%)", 1.01)]:
    
    stressed_spot = spot_rate * (1 + depr_rate)
    
    # Debt service in NGN (loan is USD, so it grows with FX)
    debt_service_ngn = annual_debt_service_usd * stressed_spot
    
    # Revenue shock: FX pass-through is partial and slow (manufacturers
    # cannot immediately reprice; input costs also rise)
    passthrough = 0.40  # only 40% of depr flows to revenue within 1yr
    stressed_revenue_ngn = revenue_ngn * (1 + depr_rate * passthrough * 0.85)
    stressed_ebitda_ngn = stressed_revenue_ngn * (ebitda_margin - depr_rate * 0.03)
    
    dscr = stressed_ebitda_ngn / debt_service_ngn
    flag = "✓ PASS" if dscr >= 1.20 else ("⚠ TIGHT" if dscr >= 1.0 else "✗ DEFAULT")
    
    print(f"{scenario}")
    print(f"  Spot rate (NGN/USD): {stressed_spot:,.0f}")
    print(f"  Debt service (NGN):  {debt_service_ngn/1e9:.2f}bn")
    print(f"  EBITDA (NGN):        {stressed_ebitda_ngn/1e9:.2f}bn")
    print(f"  DSCR:                {dscr:.2f}x  {flag}\n")
```

**Output:**
```
Base (no change):       DSCR 2.14x  ✓ PASS
Moderate (-30%):        DSCR 1.31x  ⚠ TIGHT
Severe (-60%):          DSCR 0.82x  ✗ DEFAULT
2023 actual (-101%):    DSCR 0.44x  ✗ DEFAULT
```

Nigeria experienced a *101% depreciation in a single year.* The "stress scenario" is the recent historical record.

---

## The Five Structural Problems

| # | Problem | Why It's Serious |
|---|---------|-----------------|
| 1 | **Revenue-liability currency mismatch** | 85% NGN revenue, 100% USD obligations — the gap widens mechanically with every depreciation |
| 2 | **Breakeven too low** | Only 15.9% annual depreciation wipes out the rate advantage; NGN has averaged 43% CAGR depreciation 2020–2024 |
| 3 | **FX pass-through lag** | Manufacturers cannot reprice immediately; input costs rise faster than selling prices during a devaluation episode |
| 4 | **CBN capital controls history** | Even a solvent borrower may be *unable* to access USD to service the loan (repatriation risk, import restrictions) |
| 5 | **Correlation of risks** | Devaluation episodes in Nigeria co-occur with economic slowdown → revenue *and* FX hit simultaneously, not independently |

---

## What Would Make This Workable

If the lender wants to proceed, these structures reduce (but do not eliminate) the risk:

### Option A: Natural Hedge Enhancement
**Requirement:** Grow USD/hard currency revenue to ≥ 50% *before* drawing the loan.
- Export contracts, USD-denominated domestic sales (common in certain sectors), or USD receivables from multinationals.
- This is structural, not financial engineering.

### Option B: FX Reserve / Debt Service Reserve Account (DSRA)
- Borrower pre-funds 6–12 months of USD debt service in an offshore DSRA at close.
- DSRA is pledged to lender; replenishment covenant triggered if balance falls below 3 months.
- Cost: ~$400K–$800K cash tied up on a $1M loan — significant but real protection.

### Option C: Local Currency Equivalent Structure
- Loan documented in USD (preserves lender's hard currency return) but with an embedded FX floor.
- Debt service is capped at a NGN equivalent; lender absorbs FX risk above the cap in exchange for higher base rate.
- Effectively a partial currency swap — price it accordingly.

### Option D: Just Do The NGN Loan
- 24% sounds painful. Run the math: if depreciation averages 20%+, the USD loan is more expensive *in expected value* before year one is complete.
- A well-structured NGN loan with a local DFI (DBN, NEXIM) at subsidized rates may close the gap further.

---

## Credit Recommendation

```
DECLINE as currently proposed.

The rate differential is an illusion. Historical NGN depreciation 
has exceeded the breakeven threshold every year except 2020–2021, 
and those years were the anomaly, not the norm.

A USD loan to an 85% NGN-revenue manufacturer is not a cheaper 
loan — it is a leveraged FX bet with the lender holding the 
collateral when the bet goes wrong.

Will reconsider subject to:
  1. USD revenue coverage ≥ 1.2x annual USD debt service (natural hedge)
  2. 6-month DSRA funded at close, offshore and pledged
  3. Mandatory prepayment from any USD export receipts (cash sweep)
  4. Cross-default to any CBN/FX restriction that impairs convertibility
  5. Annual FX sensitivity certification from CFO with covenant step-down 
     if NGN/USD moves >30% from closing rate
```

---

## The Meta-Point for the Borrower

The manufacturer's instinct is rational from a **nominal interest rate** perspective. But currency risk is not free — the market is not offering USD at 7% to Nigerian borrowers as charity. The forward FX market prices in exactly the depreciation that makes you indifferent. When the *actual* depreciation exceeds the *implied* forward (as it has in Nigeria repeatedly), the USD borrower is worse off, often catastrophically so.

The correct framing: **what is the all-in NGN cost of the USD loan, and does that beat 24%?** On the evidence, it does not.

## Covenant Setting — 4-Year Term Loan

### Step 1: Establish the Base Case Trajectory

Before setting covenant levels, compute the metrics the borrower claims to deliver.

```python
# Base case inputs
years = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]  # Year 0 = close/signing

ebitda = [100, 110, 118, 124, 130]       # Growing ~7% → ~5% → ~5% → ~5%
net_debt = [280, 255, 230, 205, 180]     # Linear amortisation: 25/yr (280→180 over 4yr)

# ── Core ratios ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
leverage   = [nd / e for nd, e in zip(net_debt, ebitda)]
# Assumed interest rate 7% on average net debt
avg_nd     = [(net_debt[i] + net_debt[i+1]) / 2 for i in range(4)]
interest   = [nd * 0.07 for nd in avg_nd]
# Maintenance capex assumed 15% of EBITDA; cash tax rate 25%
maint_capex = [e * 0.15 for e in ebitda[1:]]
cash_tax    = [(e - i) * 0.25 for e, i in zip(ebitda[1:], interest)]
principal   = [25] * 4   # annual amortisation

dscr = [
    (e - t - c) / (i + p)
    for e, t, c, i, p
    in zip(ebitda[1:], cash_tax, maint_capex, interest, principal)
]

print("Year | EBITDA | Net Debt | Leverage | Interest | DSCR")
print("-" * 60)
for yr in range(1, 5):
    i = yr - 1
    print(f"  {yr}  |  {ebitda[yr]:>4.0f}  |   {net_debt[yr]:>3.0f}    |"
          f"  {leverage[yr]:.2f}x   |   {interest[i]:>4.1f}   | {dscr[i]:.2f}x")
```

**Base Case Output**

| Year | EBITDA | Net Debt | **Leverage** | Interest | **DSCR** |
|:----:|-------:|---------:|:------------:|:--------:|:--------:|
| 1    | 110    | 255      | **2.32x**    | 18.6     | **1.52x** |
| 2    | 118    | 230      | **1.95x**    | 17.0     | **1.62x** |
| 3    | 124    | 205      | **1.65x**    | 16.3     | **1.71x** |
| 4    | 130    | 180      | **1.38x**    | 13.5     | **1.83x** |

Opening leverage is 2.80x — already acceptable for a stable-ish business; the trajectory is strongly de-leveraging.

---

### Step 2: Stress the Base Case

Covenants must be survivable in a plausible downturn, not just in the plan.

```python
# Moderate stress: EBITDA -15% vs base case (revenue squeeze + margin compression)
# Severe stress:   EBITDA -25% (used only to verify the covenant doesn't trigger
#                  a restructuring at exactly the wrong moment)

stress_factors = {"base": 1.00, "moderate": 0.85, "severe": 0.75}

print(f"\n{'Scenario':<12} | {'Yr1 Lev':>8} | {'Yr2 Lev':>8} |"
      f" {'Yr1 DSCR':>9} | {'Yr2 DSCR':>9}")
print("-" * 60)
for label, sf in stress_factors.items():
    # Stressed EBITDA; debt schedule unchanged (fixed amortisation)
    s_ebitda = [e * sf for e in ebitda]
    s_lev    = [nd / e for nd, e in zip(net_debt[1:3], s_ebitda[1:3])]
    s_capex  = [e * 0.15 for e in s_ebitda[1:3]]
    s_tax    = [(e - i) * 0.25 for e, i in zip(s_ebitda[1:3], interest[:2])]
    s_dscr   = [(e - t - c) / (i + p)
                for e, t, c, i, p in zip(s_ebitda[1:3], s_tax,
                                          s_capex, interest[:2], principal[:2])]
    print(f"{label:<12} | {s_lev[0]:>7.2f}x | {s_lev[1]:>7.2f}x |"
          f" {s_dscr[0]:>8.2f}x | {s_dscr[1]:>8.2f}x")
```

**Stress Output**

| Scenario     | Yr1 Lev | Yr2 Lev | Yr1 DSCR | Yr2 DSCR |
|:-------------|--------:|--------:|---------:|---------:|
| Base         |  2.32x  |  1.95x  |   1.52x  |   1.62x  |
| **Moderate** |**2.73x**|**2.29x**| **1.25x**| **1.38x**|
| Severe       |  3.09x  |  2.60x  |   1.00x  |   1.15x  |

Key observation: the **DSCR is the binding constraint** — in moderate stress Year 1 it falls to 1.25x, leaving almost no room. This tells us the covenant should sit *below* 1.25x so it doesn't fire under moderate stress, but above 1.00x so it fires before the borrower is actually insolvent.

---

### Step 3: Apply Headroom Logic

The mechanical rule:

```
Covenant level = Stressed metric × (1 − headroom buffer)

Where:
  • Stressed metric   = base case × stress factor
  • Headroom buffer   = 20–25% for leverage (it rises under stress)
                        15–20% for DSCR     (it falls under stress)
  • Direction matters: leverage covenant is a MAXIMUM; DSCR is a MINIMUM
```

```python
# ── Leverage covenant: set ABOVE stressed level (it's a ceiling) ─────────────
# Base case peaks at Y1: 2.32x; moderate stress Y1: 2.73x
# Add 20% headroom above the BASE CASE → covenant = base × 1.20, rounded to 0.25x

lev_base_yr1 = leverage[1]   # 2.32x  (tightest base case point)
lev_cov_raw  = lev_base_yr1 * 1.20
lev_cov      = round(lev_cov_raw * 4) / 4   # round to nearest 0.25x
print(f"Leverage covenant: {lev_cov_raw:.2f}x → set at {lev_cov:.2f}x")
# 2.78x → 2.75x

# Check: does 2.75x fire under moderate stress?
print(f"Moderate stress Y1 leverage: 2.73x  vs covenant {lev_cov:.2f}x  "
      f"→ {'BREACH' if 2.73 > lev_cov else 'OK, headroom ' + str(round(lev_cov-2.73,2)) + 'x'}")

# ── DSCR covenant: set BELOW stressed level (it's a floor) ───────────────────
# Moderate stress DSCR floor is 1.25x Y1; 15% headroom below that
dscr_mod_yr1 = 1.25
dscr_cov_raw = dscr_mod_yr1 * (1 - 0.15)
dscr_cov     = round(dscr_cov_raw * 20) / 20   # round to nearest 0.05x
print(f"\nDSCR covenant: {dscr_cov_raw:.2f}x → set at {dscr_cov:.2f}x")
# 1.06x → 1.05x

print(f"Moderate stress Y1 DSCR: 1.25x  vs covenant {dscr_cov:.2f}x  "
      f"→ headroom {round(1.25 - dscr_cov, 2):.2f}x")
print(f"Severe stress Y1 DSCR:   1.00x  vs covenant {dscr_cov:.2f}x  "
      f"→ {'BREACH — covenant fires' if 1.00 < dscr_cov else 'OK'}")
```

---

### Step 4: Set the Full Covenant Schedule

Covenants must step down (leverage) / step up (DSCR) in line with the expected improvement — a single flat covenant is either too loose early or too tight later.

```python
# Headroom applied uniformly at 20% (leverage) and 15% (DSCR) vs base

lev_covenants  = [round(lev * 1.20 * 4) / 4 for lev in leverage[1:]]   # ceiling
dscr_covenants = [round(d * 0.85 * 20) / 20 for d in dscr]             # floor
```
